source_text: At enim ut malum postea erupit atque inde iam coepit bonitas dei cum aduersario agere, aliud quoque negotium eadem illa iustitia dei nacta est, iam secundum aduersationem dirigendae bonitatis, ut, seposita libertate eius, qua et ultro deus bonus, pro meritis cuiusque pensetur, dignis offeratur, indignis denegetur, ingratis auferatur, proinde omnibus aemulis uindicetur. ita omne hoc iustitiae opus procuratio bonitatis est: quod iudicando damnat, quod damnando punit, quod, ut dicitis. saeuit, utique bono, non malo proficit. denique timor iudicii ad bonum, non ad malum confert. non enim sufficiebat bonum per semetipsum commendari. iam sub aduersario laborans. nam et si commendabile per semetipsum, non tamen et conseruabile, quia expugnabile iam per aduersarium, nisi uis aliqua praeesset timendi, quae bonum etiam nolentes adpetere et custodire compelleret. ceterum tot inlecebris mali expugnantibus bonum quis illud appeteret, quod impune contemneret? quis custodiret quod sine periculo amitteret? legis mali uiam latam et multo frequentiorem: nonne omnes illa laberentur. si nihil in illa timeretur? horremus terribiles minas creatoris, et uix a malo auellimur. quid, si nihil minaretur? hanc iustitiam malum dices, quae malo non fauet? hanc bonum negabis, quae bono prospicit? qualem oportet deum uelles? qualem malis expediret? sub quo delicta gauderent? cui dia- , bolus inluderet? illum bonum iudicares deum, qui hominem posset magis malum facere securitate delicti? quis boni auctor, nisi qui et exactor? proinde quis mali extraneus, nisi qui et inimicus? quis inimicus, nisi qui et expugnator? quis expugnator, nisi qui et punitor? sic totus deus bonus est, dum pro bono omnia est. sic denique omnipotens, quia et iuuandi et laedendi potens. minus est tantummodo prodesse, quia non aliud quid possit quam prodesse. de eiusmodi qua fiducia bonum sperem, si hoc solum potest? quomodo innocentiae mercedem secter, si non et nocentiae spectem? diffidam necesse est, ne nec alteram partem remuneret qui utramque non ualuit. usque adeo iustitia etiam plenitudo est diuinitatis ipsius, exhibens deum perfectum, et patrem et dominum, patrem clementia dominum disciplina, patrem potestate blanda dominum seuera, patrem diligendum pie dominum timendum necessarie, diligendum, quia malit misericordiam quam sacrificium, et timendum. quia nolit peccatum, diligendum, quia malit paenitentiam peccatoris quam mortem, et timendum, quia nolit peccatores sui iam non paenitentes. ideo lex utrumque definit : diliges deum et: timebis deum. aliud obsecutori proposuit, aliud exorbitatori.
pass_a_gloss: For but so that evil breaks out afterwards and from there now the goodness of God began to act with the adversary, also another task that same justice of God has found, now according to the adversary directing goodness, so that, having set aside the freedom of it, by which also God is good of his own accord, it is weighed according to the merits of each, it is offered to the worthy, it is denied to the unworthy, it is taken away from the ungrateful, therefore it is avenged on all rivals. thus all this work of justice is the management of goodness: which by judging condemns, which by condemning punishes, which, as you say, rages, certainly profits the good, not the evil. finally, the fear of judgment contributes to the good, not to the evil. for the good was not sufficient to be recommended by itself. now it labors under the adversary. for even if it is commendable by itself, yet it is not also preservable, because it is conquerable now by the adversary, unless some power of fear were present, which would compel even the unwilling to seek and preserve the good. but with so many allurements of evil conquering the good, who would seek that which he could despise with impunity? who would preserve that which he could lose without danger? the road of evil is broad and far more traveled: would not all stumble on it if nothing were feared on it? we tremble at the terrible threats of the creator, and we are hardly torn away from evil. what if he were threatening nothing? you will call this justice evil, which does not favor evil? you will deny this is good, which looks out for the good? what kind of god do you want? what kind would be expedient for evils? under which sins would rejoice? to which the devil would mock? you would judge that god good who could make man more evil with the security of sin? who is the author of good, if not also the exactor? therefore who is a stranger to evil, if not also an enemy? who is an enemy, if not also a conqueror? who is a conqueror, if not also a punisher? thus the whole god is good, while he is all for the good. thus finally all-powerful, because he is also powerful to help and to harm. it is less to benefit only, because he cannot do anything else than benefit. of such a kind, with what confidence can I hope for good, if he can only do this? how can I pursue the reward of innocence, if I do not also fear the punishment of guilt? I must distrust, lest he who is not able to do either part does not reward either. so far justice is also the fullness of his divinity, exhibiting god as perfect, and father and lord, father with clemency lord with discipline, father with gentle power lord with severe, father to be loved piously lord to be feared necessarily, to be loved, because he prefers mercy to sacrifice, and to be feared, because he does not want sin, to be loved, because he prefers the repentance of the sinner to death, and to be feared, because he does not want his sinners who are not repenting. therefore the law defines both: you shall love god and: you shall fear god. he has proposed one thing to the supplicant, another to the transgressor.

pass_b_english: The logic runs like this: evil erupted later, and only then did God's goodness begin to engage the adversary. That same justice of God also found another task — now directing goodness in opposition to the adversary — so that, once its freedom is set aside (the freedom by which God is good of his own accord, dispensing favor according to each person's merits: offering it to the worthy, denying it to the unworthy, withdrawing it from the ungrateful, and thereby exacting vengeance on all rivals), the whole work of justice becomes the management of goodness. What it condemns by judging, what it punishes by condemning, what you call raging — all of it profits the good, not the evil. Finally, the fear of judgment drives toward the good, not the evil. For goodness did not suffice to commend itself; now it labors under the adversary. Even if it is commendable in itself, it is not also preservable, because it is now conquerable by the adversary — unless some power of fear were present to compel even the unwilling to seek and guard the good. With so many allurements of evil conquering the good, who would pursue what he could despise with impunity? Who would guard what he could lose without danger? The road of evil is broad and far more traveled: would not everyone stumble onto it if nothing were feared on it? We tremble at the Creator's terrible threats, and we are hardly torn away from evil. What if he threatened nothing? Would you call this justice evil because it does not favor evil? Would you deny this is good because it looks out for the good? What kind of god do you want? What kind would suit evildoers? Under whom would sins rejoice? At whom would the devil mock? Would you judge that god good who could make man more evil by the security of sin? Who is the author of good, if not also the exactor? Therefore who is a stranger to evil, if not also an enemy? Who is an enemy, if not also a conqueror? Who is a conqueror, if not also a punisher? Thus the whole God is good, so long as he is entirely for the good. Thus finally he is all-powerful, because he is powerful both to help and to harm. It is less to be only beneficial, because he can do nothing else but benefit. With what confidence could I hope for good from such a one, if he can only do that? How could I pursue the reward of innocence, if I do not also fear the punishment of guilt? I must distrust, lest the one who lacked the power for either part fail to reward either. So far justice is also the fullness of divinity itself, exhibiting God as perfect — both Father and Lord: Father by clemency, Lord by discipline; Father with gentle power, Lord with severity; Father to be loved piously, Lord to be feared necessarily — to be loved because he prefers mercy to sacrifice, and to be feared because he does not want sin; to be loved because he prefers the sinner's repentance to death, and to be feared because he does not want his sinners who are no longer repenting. Therefore the law defines both: you shall love God, and you shall fear God. He set one thing before the supplicant, another before the transgressor.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex rhetorical structure of Tertullian's argument regarding the relationship between God's goodness and justice. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause rendering, and Pass B provides a polished, coherent version that maintains the nuances of the Latin (e.g., 'obsecutori' as 'supplicant' and 'exorbitatori' as 'transgressor').

source: 'At enim ut malum postea erupit atque inde iam coepit bonitas dei cum aduersario agere', English: 'For but so that evil breaks out afterwards and from there now the goodness of God began to act with the adversary'
